name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Statement not applicable to reverse osmosis

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements does not apply to reverse osmosis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Osmosis is the spontaneous, passive movement of solvent molecules across a semipermeable membrane from a region of higher water potential (lower solute concentration) to a region of lower water potential (higher solute concentration).

Step 2: Evaluation
Reverse osmosis forces solvent molecules to move in the opposite direction—from a concentrated solution to pure solvent or a dilute solution—by applying an external hydrostatic pressure greater than the osmotic pressure of the solution. Because external mechanical energy/pressure must be supplied to drive the solvent against its natural osmotic gradient, reverse osmosis is an active (energy-requiring) process, widely used for water purification and desalination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, describing reverse osmosis as a passive process does not apply to it.

answer.text: In this technique, pressure greater than osmotic pressure is applied to the system

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Factor not directly affecting transpiration

questiontext.text: Which one of the following will not directly affect transpiration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transpiration is the evaporative loss of water from aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata. Its rate is governed by external environmental factors (temperature, light, relative humidity, and wind speed) and internal plant factors (number and distribution of stomata, percent of open stomata, water status of the plant, and canopy structure).

Step 2: Evaluation
Temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules and vapor pressure deficit, directly increasing evaporation. Light triggers stomatal opening and warms the leaf, directly affecting transpiration. Wind speed removes the boundary layer of humid air around the leaf, directly increasing the transpiration rate. Chlorophyll content of leaves is essential for photosynthesis, not for the physical evaporation of water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the chlorophyll content of leaves will not directly affect transpiration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Leaf type with more lower stomata

questiontext.text: The lower surface of leaf will have more number of stomata in a

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leaves are classified based on the distribution of stomata and internal anatomy into dorsiventral (typically dicot) leaves and isobilateral (typically monocot) leaves.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a dorsiventral leaf, the upper (adaxial) surface is directly exposed to sunlight, so having fewer stomata on the upper surface and a greater number of stomata on the shaded lower (abaxial) surface helps minimize excessive water loss by transpiration. In contrast, an isobilateral leaf has stomata distributed almost equally on both surfaces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the lower surface of a leaf has a greater number of stomata in a dorsiventral leaf.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Form of sugar transported in phloem

questiontext.text: The form of sugar transported through phloem is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem translocates photosynthates (sugars) from source tissues (such as mature leaves) to sink tissues (such as roots, fruits, and growing regions).

Step 2: Evaluation
Sucrose is a non-reducing disaccharide, making it chemically inert and stable during long-distance transport through sieve tubes without reacting with other cellular components or being readily metabolized along the pathway. Glucose, fructose, and ribose are reducing monosaccharides that are chemically more reactive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the form of sugar transported through phloem is sucrose.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Conditions under which guttation takes place

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Guttation is the loss of water in the form of liquid droplets from specialized pores called hydathodes located at the margins or tips of leaves in herbaceous plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Guttation is driven by positive hydrostatic pressure (root pressure) built up in the xylem when water absorption by roots continues while water loss by transpiration is minimal, such as at night or early morning in humid conditions. If transpiration is high, water evaporates as vapour and root pressure cannot build up to push liquid water out.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, guttation takes place when the root pressure is high and the rate of transpiration is low.

answer.text: when the root pressure is high and the rate of transpiration is low.
when the root pressure is low and the rate of transpiration is high
when the root pressure equals the rate of transpiration
when the root pressure as well as rate of transpiration are high.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Example of imbibition in plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of imbibition

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Imbibition is a special type of diffusion in which water is adsorbed by solids or colloids (such as proteins, starch, and cellulose), causing them to increase enormously in volume without forming a solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Dry seeds contain hydrophilic colloids that adsorb water from moist soil, leading to swelling and generating imbibition pressure that helps the seedling emerge. In contrast, uptake of water by root hair occurs by osmosis, exchange of gases in stomata occurs by simple diffusion, and opening of stomata is regulated by turgor changes in guard cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, swelling of seed when put in soil is an example of imbibition.

answer.text: swelling of seed when put in soil

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Fate of nutrients during plant senescence

questiontext.text: When a plant undergoes senescence, the nutrients may be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Senescence is the programmed ageing and deterioration of plant organs (such as older leaves) prior to abscission or death.

Step 2: Evaluation
Before senescent parts die and are shed, mobile mineral ions (such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium) and organic nutrients are remobilized from the older, dying tissues and transported through the phloem to younger, actively growing parts such as apical buds, young leaves, and developing fruits or seeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, when a plant undergoes senescence, the nutrients may be translocated.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Water potential of pure water at standard temperature

questiontext.text: Water potential of pure water at standard temperature is equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water potential (\(\Psi_w\)) is a measure of the free energy of water molecules per unit volume, relative to pure water at standard temperature and atmospheric pressure (not under any external pressure).

Step 2: Evaluation
By convention, pure water has the maximum water potential and is assigned a value of zero (\(\Psi_w = 0\)). Addition of solutes lowers the free energy of water, making the solute potential (\(\Psi_s\)) and thus the water potential of any solution at atmospheric pressure negative.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the water potential of pure water at standard temperature is equal to zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Functions of mycorrhiza in plant roots

questiontext.text:
Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association of fungus with root system which helps in

A. Absorption of water
B. Mineral nutrition
C. Translocation
D. Gaseous exchange

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mycorrhiza is a mutually beneficial symbiotic association between a fungus and the root system of higher plants (such as Pinus).

Step 2: Evaluation
The fungal hyphae form a dense network around the young roots and penetrate the cortical cells, greatly increasing the surface area for absorption of water and minerals (especially phosphorus) from the soil. In return, the plant roots provide sugars and nitrogen-containing compounds to the fungus. Translocation within vascular bundles and gaseous exchange through stomata or lenticels are not primary functions of mycorrhiza.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, mycorrhiza helps in both absorption of water and mineral nutrition.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Osmosis across semipermeable membrane between chambers

questiontext.text: Based on the figure given below which of the following statements is not correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows two chambers, A and B, separated by a semi-permeable membrane. Chamber A contains water with fewer solute molecules (lower solute concentration), while chamber B contains water with many solute molecules (higher solute concentration).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both chambers are at atmospheric pressure, and the membrane is selectively permeable only to the solvent (water), not to the solute molecules.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Water potential is given by \(\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\). During osmosis, water (solvent) moves across a semi-permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential (less negative \(\Psi_s\), lower solute concentration) to a region of lower water potential (more negative \(\Psi_s\), higher solute concentration). The direction and rate of osmosis depend on both the pressure gradient and the concentration gradient.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since chamber A has a lower solute concentration than chamber B, chamber A has a higher water potential than chamber B. Consequently, solvent (water) molecules diffuse from chamber A to chamber B across the semi-permeable membrane. A semi-permeable membrane is a prerequisite for osmosis, and it prevents the passage of solute molecules from either chamber to the other.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Stating that movement of solute will take place from chamber A to B violates the selectivity of the semi-permeable membrane and the concentration gradient of solute (which is already higher in B). Therefore, the incorrect statement is that movement of solute will take place from A to B.

answer.text: Movement of solvent molecules will take place from chamber A to B.
Movement of solute will take place from A to B.
Presence of a semipermeable is a pre-requisite for this process to occur.
The direction and rate of osmosis depends on both the pressure gradient and concentration gradient.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Matching plant structures and physiological processes

questiontext.text:
Match the followings and choose the correct option

Column IColumn II
A. Leavesi. Anti-transpirant
B. Seedii. Transpiration
C. Rootsiii. Negative osmotic potential
D. Aspiriniv. Imbibition
E. Plasmolyzed cellv. Absorption

Options:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each plant organ, chemical agent, or cellular state is associated with a characteristic physiological phenomenon in water relations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Leaves are the primary sites of transpiration (evaporative water loss through stomata). Dry seeds absorb water by imbibition during germination. Roots are specialized for the absorption of water and minerals from the soil. Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) induces stomatal closure and acts as an anti-transpirant. A plasmolyzed cell has lost water to a hypertonic solution, resulting in a concentrated cell sap with a negative osmotic potential.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching pairs are: Leaves with Transpiration (A-ii), Seed with Imbibition (B-iv), Roots with Absorption (C-v), Aspirin with Anti-transpirant (D-i), and Plasmolyzed cell with Negative osmotic potential (E-iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Mismatched pair among plant plastids

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plastids are plant organelles classified according to their pigments and stored nutrients into chloroplasts, chromoplasts, and leucoplasts (which are colourless plastids specialized for storage: amyloplasts, elaioplasts, and aleuroplasts).

Step 2: Evaluation
Amyloplasts store carbohydrates (starch), whereas protein granules are stored by aleuroplasts. Elaioplasts store oils and fats. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll pigments for photosynthesis. Chromoplasts contain coloured carotenoid pigments other than chlorophyll. Leucoplasts are colourless plastids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, pairing amyloplast with storing protein granules is the mismatched pair.

answer.text: Chromoplasts : contain coloured pigments other than chlorophyll
